claims.text: The starting material is an as-deposited, nanocrystalline, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy-alloy thin film or patterned nanoribbon on a rigid substrate.
The as-deposited material contains residual stress generated during deposition.
Substrate clamping produces persistent interfacial strain gradients in the thin film.
Substrate-induced strain and localized lattice distortions stabilize a metastable magnetic or crystallographic phase.
The strain-stabilized metastable phase suppresses a field-induced phase transformation.
Suppression of the phase transformation reduces latent-heat exchange.
Reduced latent-heat exchange diminishes the magnetocaloric effect.
Substrate-induced interfacial strain increases hysteresis during magnetic-cooling cycles.
Limited heat transfer in the nanostructured state slows the reversible transformation.
Slower transformation caused by limited heat transfer exacerbates hysteretic losses.
Selective substrate removal or reduced interfacial clamping will relieve substrate-induced strain in the nanoribbons.
Freestanding nanoribbons will exhibit a larger magnetic entropy change than otherwise identical substrate-bound nanoribbons.
Freestanding nanoribbons will exhibit less hysteresis than otherwise identical substrate-bound nanoribbons.
Relieving substrate clamping will make the nanoribbon magnetocaloric response more similar to that of bulk material.
The proposed clamping effect is expected primarily for films or nanoribbons thinner than approximately 200 nm.
The predicted behavior applies near room temperature under low applied fields of approximately 0.1 T or less.
Thicker films or bulk forms may behave differently from sub-200-nm films and nanoribbons.
Nanodefect pinning may counteract the improvement expected from releasing substrate clamping.
Heat-transfer bottlenecks may counteract the improvement expected from releasing substrate clamping and limit cycle frequency.
